opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the questions we're trying to answer with Humane Evals don't belong to any single field.

When people evaluate AI systems today, the dominant approach comes out of machine learning: benchmarks, accuracy scores, capability tests. Those matter, but they mostly ask whether a system can do a task. They're much less good at asking what the system does *to people* over time. Does it foster dependence? Does it flatter someone into a worse decision? Does it quietly erode a teenager's sense of their own judgment? Those are fundamentally human questions, and the people who have spent careers studying them are developmental psychologists, clinicians, sociologists, ethicists, human-computer interaction researchers, and people who study persuasion and attention.

The problem is that these communities often don't talk to each other. A psychologist might have a deep, validated way of thinking about something like unhealthy attachment, but no idea how to turn that into something you can run against a language model at scale. Meanwhile an ML engineer can build an evaluation pipeline in an afternoon but may not know what they should actually be measuring, or how to tell a meaningful signal from a superficial one. Each side holds half the puzzle.

So connecting them is the work, not a nice extra. We want evaluations that are rigorous enough that engineers and companies take them seriously, and grounded enough in real human experience that they measure what actually matters for wellbeing. You only get both when people from those different worlds sit down together, argue about definitions, and build something neither could have built alone.

There's also a practical reason. Evaluations shape incentives. Whatever gets measured is what labs end up optimizing for. If the only things measured are capability and narrow safety, that's what we'll get more of. By bringing a wider range of expertise into how evals are designed, we're trying to widen what the industry considers worth optimizing for, so that respecting human agency, attention, and relationships becomes part of what "a good model" means.

r001.rationale: The response explains that psychologists contribute validated ways to understand human outcomes, while ML engineers contribute evaluation pipelines, and that both are needed to build useful Humane Evals.

r002.rationale: It describes a methodological divide: psychologists may not know how to operationalize research at scale, while ML engineers may not know what to measure or how to distinguish meaningful signals from superficial ones.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that no single discipline can see the whole problem. If you want to know whether a technology is actually good for people, you need psychologists who understand attention and wellbeing, sociologists who understand how norms shift, economists who understand incentives, and computer scientists who can actually build the measurement into the system. Each of those groups has been studying pieces of this for years, often in isolation, using different vocabularies and different standards of evidence.

What we kept noticing is that the gaps between those fields are exactly where harm hides. A metric that looks fine to an engineer might be a red flag to a developmental psychologist. A finding that's well established in the behavioral literature might never make it into a product review because nobody translated it into something an evaluation could test. So Humane Evals is really an attempt to build a shared language and a shared set of benchmarks, so that insight from one corner of the research world can become a practical check in another.

There's also a credibility point. If the evaluations we propose only come from one perspective, they're easy to dismiss as ideological or impractical. When they're grounded in work across many fields and co-designed with people who will actually use them, they're much harder to wave away. And frankly, the researchers themselves want this. Many of them have been working on these questions for a long time and have felt like they were shouting into the void. Giving them a place to connect and compound each other's work is as much the point as any single eval we publish.

r001.rationale: The response says no single discipline can see the whole problem and gives complementary roles for psychologists, sociologists, economists, and computer scientists.

r002.rationale: It describes researchers working in isolation with different vocabularies and standards of evidence, presenting those differences as gaps Humane Evals aims to bridge.

astra-6.text:
Because the effects of technology don’t fit neatly within any one discipline. A computer scientist might assess what a system can do, while a psychologist asks how it affects someone’s thinking or relationships, and a social scientist looks at what happens across communities and institutions. We need those perspectives in conversation to understand what we should actually be evaluating.

For me, that’s central to Humane Evals: connecting technical capabilities to human consequences. If we only measure what’s easy to measure, we can miss the things that matter most. Bringing researchers together helps us ask better questions, challenge our assumptions, and develop evaluations that reflect the complexity of people’s lives.

r001.rationale: The response says technology’s effects span disciplines and gives complementary roles for computer scientists, psychologists, and social scientists, whose perspectives need to be brought together.

r002.rationale: It describes different disciplinary questions and the value of connecting perspectives, but does not identify differences in research methodology as a challenge to making that connection.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the effects of AI don’t fit neatly into any one discipline. A technical researcher might be able to measure what a model can do, but understanding what that means for people requires perspectives from psychology, the social sciences, and people who understand the context in which it’s being used.

With Humane Evals, the idea is to bring those perspectives together so we’re asking better questions in the first place. What should we be testing for? What might a conventional benchmark miss? Connecting researchers helps us turn concerns about human well-being into things we can actually investigate and evaluate.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluating AI’s effects on people requires perspectives from technical research, psychology, social sciences, and contextual expertise, and that Humane Evals brings them together.

r002.rationale: It describes the need for multiple perspectives but does not identify differences in researchers’ methodologies as a challenge to connecting them.
